additions.reason: The Rebbe explicitly states that each foreign thought IS a klipah — a direct bechina identification. The klipah is a complete spiritual stature, making it the evil domain's structural unit in this Torah.
additions.source_quote: כִּי כָל מַחֲשָׁבָה זָרָה הוּא קְלִפָּה, וְהִיא קוֹמָה שְׁלֵמָה

additions.reason: The Rebbe explicitly states twice that each foreign thought (= klipah) IS a complete spiritual stature (קומה שלמה), citing an established Kabbalistic teaching ('כַּמּוּבָא'). This concept is the structural description of the klipah's spiritual reality — making it a third face of the same evil domain entity.
additions.source_quote: כָּל מַחֲשָׁבָה וּמַחֲשָׁבָה הִיא קוֹמָה שְׁלֵמָה, כַּמּוּבָא

additions.reason: Prayer in order (כסדר) is the central positive act of the Torah. It is the structural equivalent of the warrior's march — by praying in sequence without interruption, the person defeats the foreign thoughts. The phrase 'כְּשֶׁמִּתְפַּלְּלִין כְּסֵדֶר' defines the essential mode of victorious prayer.
additions.source_quote: כְּשֶׁהָאָדָם עוֹמֵד וּמִתְפַּלֵּל כְּסֵדֶר וְאֵינוֹ מַשְׁגִּיחַ עַל הַמַּחֲשָׁבוֹת זָרוֹת... הוּא מְנַצֵּחַ אוֹתָם

additions.reason: The 'path of his walking' (דֶּרֶךְ הִלּוּכוֹ) is the bechina of prayer in order. It is the same concept stated in the metaphor's language — the warrior walks through, the praying person walks through his prayer. The cutting/defeat happens by this walking, not by any separate act.
additions.source_quote: אֲזַי בְּדֶרֶךְ הִלּוּכוֹ בִּתְפִלָּתוֹ הוּא מַפִּיל אוֹתָם

additions.reason: The warrior (גִּבּוֹר) is introduced in the mashal as the one who can walk through ambushers. This is the essential spiritual quality that the praying person must embody — inner strength and resolution. In the nimshal (application), this is the quality of one who strengthens himself to pray in order ('כְּשֶׁמִּתְגַּבֵּר לְהִתְפַּלֵּל כְּסֵדֶר').
additions.source_quote: וּכְשֶׁהוּא גִּבּוֹר וְעֹבֵר בֵּינֵיהֶם, אֲזַי בְּדֶרֶךְ הִלּוּכוֹ הוּא מַפִּיל אוֹתָם

additions.reason: Not-attending (אֵינוֹ מַשְׁגִּיחַ) to the foreign thoughts is the bechina of the forward-moving stance. The Rebbe states it as the essential technique: not looking back (לִבְלִי לְהַבִּיט לְאַחֲרָיו), which is how the foreign thoughts depart by themselves (מִמֵּילָא יִסְתַּלְּקוּ). The non-looking IS the movement — they are two expressions of the same inner stance.
additions.source_quote: אֵין צְרִיכִין לְהִסְתַּכֵּל עֲלֵיהֶם כְּלָל, רַק לֵילֵךְ כְּסֵדֶר בִּתְפִלָּתוֹ וְלִבְלִי לְהַבִּיט לְאַחֲרָיו כְּלָל, וְעַל־יְדֵי־זֶה מִמֵּילָא יִסְתַּלְּקוּ

eitza_relationships_identified.description: Prayer in order CAUSES (eitza) the defeat of foreign thoughts — not a bechina. The prayer is not the same thing as the defeat; the prayer produces the defeat.
Not attending to the thoughts CAUSES (eitza) them to depart by themselves — causal chain, not bechina.

analysis_notes.metaphor_analysis: The text contains a mashal (parable) about מִלְחָמָה (war), רוֹצְחִים וְאוֹרְבִים (murderers and ambushers), and אֵיבָרִים (limbs — יָד, רֶגֶל). These are structural metaphors (nimshal/mashal pairing), not independent theological concepts connected by bechina. They are not candidates for separate packages: they are the narrative vehicle for the two substantive domains (foreign thoughts = evil; prayer movement = good). No separate 'war metaphor' package is warranted.
